## Related Work {#sec-related-work}

Conformal prediction provides finite-sample predictive-coverage guarantees under exchangeability [@vovk2005algorithmic; @lei2018distributionfree]. Weighted conformal variants extend this logic to covariate shift when the shift mechanism can be estimated [@tibshirani2019covariate]. Conformalized quantile regression calibrates quantile-regression estimates to retain finite-sample coverage [@romano2019conformalized], and adaptive conformal inference addresses distribution shift over time [@gibbs2021adaptive]. These guarantees do not by themselves certify a reliability benchmark. If the information set includes recent labels, dataset identity, or bookkeeping fields unavailable in the intended decision setting, nominal coverage can describe the constructed benchmark rather than the intended threshold-decision problem. The localized-residual analysis used here is only a diagnostic inspired by this literature, not an implementation of density-ratio weighted conformal prediction.

Battery SOH and remaining useful life (RUL) studies increasingly report probabilistic forecasts, predictive intervals, and prognostic performance under uncertainty [@saxena2010evaluating; @he2011remaining; @liu2020futurecapacity], and real-application SOH estimation has its own mature methodological literature [@berecibar2016critical]. A parallel transfer-learning literature studies how SOH estimators adapt across batteries, operating conditions, and laboratory or field domains [@ye2021domainadversarial; @vilsen2022field; @shen2024review]. These studies motivate cross-domain evaluation, but they usually treat the benchmark schema as a prerequisite for model comparison rather than as the primary object of reliability analysis.

The benchmark-integrity concern is also connected to broader machine-learning reliability work on dataset documentation, shortcut learning, and leakage [@gebru2021datasheets; @geirhos2020shortcut; @kapoor2023leakage]. Those literatures warn that apparent predictive performance can be driven by unintended signals or by data-splitting and feature-availability choices. In a battery SOH benchmark, the corresponding risk is not merely a statistical nuisance: a feature-schema artifact can be mistaken for protocol drift, or a recent-label proxy can make a maintenance-facing forecast look reliable under conditions that are unavailable at decision time.

This paper therefore occupies a narrower gap. It is not a new SOH estimator and not a broad survey of battery transfer learning. It is a measurement-validity case study: the unit of analysis is the reliability of the benchmark evidence itself, especially how conformal interval behavior changes across recent-label, split, schema-bundle, residual-drift, and SOH-threshold diagnostics.
